---
title: "Lists"
---

::: {.callout-note}

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- **Describe** the characteristics of an R list.
- **Describe** important use-cases for lists, and **explain** why lists are the best choice in these situations.
- **Create** new lists in R.
- **Access and modify** list elements using different methods, and **explain** the difference between the available
  selection operators (`$`, `[]`, `[[]]`).

:::

Lists are one of R's most versatile and ubiquitous data structures. Like vectors, lists are one-dimensional objects.
Unlike vectors, however, lists can comprise arbitrary mixes of data objects with any combination of types. This
flexibility makes lists particularly useful for storing and organizing heterogeneous data such as the results returned
from statistical modeling functions.

This is a genuinely new step up from what you've learned so far. Vectors and matrices both required every element to
share the same type. Lists remove that restriction entirely. Understanding *why* you'd reach for a list instead of
a vector (not just *how* to create one) is one of the main goals of this tutorial.

## Why Use a List?

A few common situations where a list is the natural (or only) choice:

- **Storing mixed-type information about one "thing."** If you want to keep someone's name (text), age (number), and
  active status (logical) bundled together as a single object, a vector can't do that. It would coerce everything
  to one shared type. A list keeps each piece in its original type.
- **Storing the results of a complex function.** Many R functions (especially statistical modeling functions you'll
  encounter later) return dozens of pieces of output at once, coefficients, fitted values, diagnostic statistics,
  the original data, all of different shapes and types. A list is the only structure flexible enough to hold all of
  that in one object.
- **Building nested or hierarchical data.** Since a list can contain other lists, they're a natural fit for data
  that has its own internal structure, like a set of survey responses grouped by respondent.

You'll see the second data structure in the next tutorial, the *data frame*, is actually a special, constrained
kind of list. So getting comfortable with lists now will make data frames feel much less mysterious later.

## Quick Check

In your own words: why can't you just use a vector to store someone's name, age, and active status together?
